title: The history of AI video models
tagline: From a row of cameras photographing a galloping horse in 1878 to models that turn a sentence into a talking film clip, and the rules that followed.
intro: Video has always been a stack of still pictures shown quickly. For decades computers could only play such stacks back. Then networks learned to invent images, diffusion learned to turn static into pictures, and transformers learned to handle patches of space and time together. By 2024 a sentence could become a realistic clip, and governments, India among them, began requiring labels on AI-made video.

eras.name: Moving pictures
eras.summary: Photographers and film-makers learn that motion is just many still pictures shown quickly, and settle on 24 of them per second.

eras.name: Networks learn to imagine
eras.summary: Neural networks learn to invent images and the first tiny videos, and face-swapped "deepfakes" appear.

eras.name: From noise to pictures
eras.summary: Diffusion turns static into images, works in a compressed latent space, follows prompts and starts making short videos.

eras.name: Video for everyone
eras.summary: Text-to-video tools reach the public, clips get longer, sharper and gain sound, and their cost becomes clear.

eras.name: Labels and laws
eras.summary: Watermarks, content credentials and new laws in India, China and Europe try to make AI video easy to recognise.

events.title: A galloping horse, frame by frame
events.who: Eadweard Muybridge
events.text: Muybridge lined up a row of cameras along a racetrack, each fired by a thread as the horse ran past. The sequence proved that all four hooves leave the ground at once. Shown quickly one after another, the still photos looked like motion.
events.why: It showed that movement can be stored as a stack of still pictures, the idea every video still uses.

events.title: 24 frames every second
events.who: The film industry, with the arrival of sound films
events.text: When films gained soundtracks in the late 1920s, projectors had to run at one steady speed so voices sounded right. The industry settled on 24 frames per second, which is still the standard for cinema.
events.why: A single minute of film is 1,440 separate pictures, which is why video is so much bigger than one image.

events.title: Two networks play a game
events.who: Ian Goodfellow and colleagues
events.text: In a generative adversarial network (GAN), one network makes fake images and another tries to spot them. Each gets better by competing with the other. A year earlier, Kingma and Welling had shown the variational autoencoder, another way to generate pictures.
events.why: For the first time, networks could invent new, realistic-looking images instead of only sorting them.

events.title: Learning to undo noise
events.who: Jascha Sohl-Dickstein, Eric Weiss, Niru Maheswaranathan and Surya Ganguli
events.text: Borrowing an idea from physics, the team slowly destroyed images by adding noise, then trained a network to run the process backwards. The results were blurry and the idea was mostly ignored for five years.
events.why: It was the seed of diffusion, the method behind most video models today.

events.title: The first tiny AI videos
events.who: Carl Vondrick, Hamed Pirsiavash and Antonio Torralba
events.text: Trained on over two million unlabelled videos, VGAN generated clips of 32 frames at 64 by 64 pixels, up to about a second long. It learned to draw a still background and a moving foreground separately. The paper appeared at NeurIPS 2016.
events.why: It showed a network could learn how scenes move, not just how they look.

events.title: The word "deepfake"
events.who: An anonymous Reddit user
events.text: A user called "deepfakes" posted videos in which one person's face had been swapped onto another's using neural networks, and shared the code. The name stuck for any AI-faked video. Most early deepfakes targeted women without their consent.
events.why: Faked video became a public worry years before text-to-video models existed.

events.title: Diffusion finally works
events.who: Jonathan Ho, Ajay Jain and Pieter Abbeel
events.text: Denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPM) trained a network to predict the noise hidden in a picture, then removed it step by step, starting from pure static. The images matched the best GANs, and training was much more stable.
events.why: Almost every image and video generator since is built on this recipe.

events.title: A label that travels with the file
events.who: Adobe, Arm, BBC, Intel, Microsoft and Truepic
events.text: Six organisations formed the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) to write an open standard for "content credentials": signed records, attached to a file, of who made it and how it was edited. Many AI tools later used it to mark their output.
events.why: It gave the world a shared way to say where a picture or video came from.

events.title: Do the work in a smaller space
events.who: Robin Rombach, Andreas Blattmann, Dominik Lorenz, Patrick Esser and Björn Ommer
events.where: LMU Munich and Heidelberg University, Germany
events.text: Instead of denoising every pixel, latent diffusion first squeezes an image with an autoencoder into a much smaller grid of numbers, the "latent". Diffusion happens there, and a decoder turns the result back into pixels. This cut the cost dramatically.
events.why: Video models compress in the same way, in both space and time, or they could never afford to run.

events.title: Turning up the prompt
events.who: Jonathan Ho and Tim Salimans
events.text: Classifier-free guidance trains one model both with and without the text prompt. At each step it pushes the picture further in the direction the prompt suggests. First shown at a NeurIPS workshop, it was posted on arXiv in July 2022.
events.why: It is the "follow the prompt more closely" dial inside nearly every text-to-image and text-to-video model.

events.title: Diffusion for video
events.who: Jonathan Ho, Tim Salimans, Alexey Gritsenko, William Chan, Mohammad Norouzi and David Fleet
events.text: Video Diffusion Models denoised all the frames of a short clip together, so each frame could "see" its neighbours. This kept objects steadier from frame to frame than making each frame separately.
events.why: Denoising frames together is the main trick for keeping video consistent.

events.title: Stable Diffusion is released openly
events.who: Stability AI, CompVis at LMU Munich and Runway
events.where: Munich, Germany and London, United Kingdom
events.text: A latent diffusion model trained on billions of captioned images was released with its weights, so anyone with a gaming graphics card could run it at home. Thousands of tools and many later open video models were built on it.
events.why: Image generation went from lab demo to something millions of people could use and study.

events.title: Make-A-Video
events.who: Uriel Singer, Adam Polyak, Devi Parikh, Yaniv Taigman and colleagues at Meta AI
events.where: Tel Aviv, Israel and Menlo Park, United States
events.text: Meta's team took a text-to-image model and taught it motion from videos that had no captions at all. It produced short, low-resolution clips from a sentence.
events.why: It showed video models could borrow what image models already knew about the world.

events.title: Imagen Video
events.who: Jonathan Ho, William Chan, Chitwan Saharia and colleagues at Google
events.text: A chain of seven diffusion models first made a small, jerky clip, then filled in extra frames and added detail. The paper reports 128 frames at 1280 by 768 pixels and 24 frames per second, about 5.3 seconds.
events.why: It reached HD resolution by building a clip up in stages.

events.title: Diffusion meets the transformer
events.who: William Peebles and Saining Xie
events.where: UC Berkeley and New York University, United States
events.text: The diffusion transformer (DiT) cut the latent into small patches and processed them with a transformer, the same design behind chatbots. Bigger transformers gave better pictures, predictably.
events.why: This design, scaled up to patches of space and time, became the backbone of Sora and many later video models.

events.title: Text-to-video anyone can try
events.who: Runway
events.text: Runway announced Gen-2, which made short clips of about four seconds from a text prompt or an image. It opened to the public in stages over the following months and was widely described as the first publicly available text-to-video model.
events.why: Artists and students began experimenting with AI video themselves.

events.title: An invisible watermark
events.who: Google DeepMind
events.text: SynthID hid a signal inside AI-made images from Google's Imagen model. People cannot see it, but a detector can find it, even after cropping or compression. In May 2024 Google said it would extend SynthID to video made by Veo.
events.why: Watermarks inside the pixels can survive where a visible label is easily cropped off.

events.title: India warns platforms about deepfakes
events.who: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY)
events.text: In November 2023 a deepfake video of a well-known actor spread widely, and ministers called deepfakes a dangerous form of misinformation. In December MeitY advised all platforms to tell users clearly, at sign-up and when they upload, that impersonation and deceptive content are banned under the IT Rules.
events.why: India began treating deepfakes as a problem platforms must actively deal with.

events.title: Sora: up to a minute of video
events.who: OpenAI
events.text: OpenAI showed Sora, which it reported could make videos up to one minute long. Its technical report described compressing video into a latent space and cutting it into "spacetime patches" for a diffusion transformer. It was not released to the public at first.
events.why: It showed how far scaling a diffusion transformer on video could go, and set off a race.

events.title: Labels for AI-made content in India
events.who: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY)
events.text: A 1 March advisory asked platforms to seek government permission before offering untested AI models, and to mark AI-made content that could be used as a deepfake with a permanent unique identifier or metadata. After criticism, a 15 March advisory dropped the permission step but kept the call for labels.
events.why: It was India's first push for AI content labels, a step towards later rules.

events.title: Veo, with watermarks built in
events.who: Google DeepMind
events.text: Google announced Veo, which it reported could make 1080p videos beyond a minute long. Its videos were to carry SynthID watermarks. Veo 2 followed in December 2024.
events.why: Big labs began shipping watermarking alongside video models.

events.title: Kling from China
events.who: Kuaishou
events.text: Kuaishou, a short-video company, launched Kling for testing in China. It reported clips up to two minutes long at 1080p and 30 frames per second. Kling soon opened to users around the world.
events.why: Strong video models were now coming from several countries, not one lab.

events.title: Sora opens, and open models catch up
events.who: OpenAI; Tencent
events.where: San Francisco, United States and Shenzhen, China
events.text: On 9 December OpenAI opened Sora to paying users in some countries, with clips up to 1080p and 20 seconds. The same month Tencent released HunyuanVideo, a 13-billion-parameter model with openly published weights, after Tsinghua University and Zhipu AI's open CogVideoX in August.
events.why: Anyone could now study how a large video model is built, not just use one.

events.title: Pictures and sound in one go
events.who: Google DeepMind
events.text: Google announced Veo 3, which generated speech, sound effects and music together with the video in a single model. Widely shared clips of talking characters made it hard to tell AI video from real footage at a glance.
events.why: Realistic talking video made labels and provenance more urgent.

events.title: Counting the energy of a video
events.who: MIT Technology Review; Hugging Face researchers
events.text: Measurements on one open model found a 5-second clip used about 3.4 million joules, more than 700 times a high-quality image. A Hugging Face study found that doubling a video's length roughly quadruples the energy needed.
events.why: Video is the most energy-hungry thing most people ask AI to make.

events.title: China requires AI labels
events.who: Cyberspace Administration of China and three other agencies
events.text: China's labelling measures took effect, requiring visible labels on AI-made content such as video, plus hidden labels in the file's data. In Europe, the AI Act's Article 50 requires AI-made deepfakes to be disclosed, with those rules applying from August 2026.
events.why: Several large markets moved from asking to requiring AI labels.

events.title: Sora 2 and an app
events.who: OpenAI
events.text: OpenAI released Sora 2, which added synchronised speech and sound, in a social app where people could put themselves into videos. It spread quickly, and so did complaints about copyright and look-alike videos of real people.
events.why: AI video became something people shared in a feed, raising new questions about consent.

events.title: India drafts rules for synthetic media
events.who: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY)
events.text: MeitY published draft amendments to the IT Rules defining "synthetically generated information". The draft proposed that visible labels cover at least 10% of the screen, or play during the first 10% of an audio clip, and asked the public for comments.
events.why: It was the first draft Indian law written specifically about AI-made media.

events.title: India's deepfake rules become law
events.who: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY)
events.text: The amended IT Rules, in force from 20 February 2026, require AI-made audio and video to carry a prominent label and metadata that platforms must not strip. The fixed 10% size was dropped. Platforms must remove unlawful content within 3 hours of a lawful order, and non-consensual intimate images, including deepfakes, within 2 hours.
events.why: India now has some of the world's strictest labelling and takedown rules for AI video.

events.title: Sora is switched off
events.who: OpenAI
events.text: OpenAI announced it would close the Sora app, which shut on 26 April 2026, with the API ending in September. News reports pointed to very high running costs and problems with copyright and deepfakes.
events.why: Making video is expensive, and even a famous product could not cover its costs.

people.name: Eadweard Muybridge
people.note: Photographed a galloping horse with a row of cameras in 1878, showing motion as a sequence of stills.

people.name: Ian Goodfellow
people.note: Invented generative adversarial networks in 2014, which powered early image generators, video GANs and deepfakes.

people.name: Jascha Sohl-Dickstein
people.note: Led the 2015 paper that first used diffusion, adding and removing noise, to generate images.

people.name: Jonathan Ho
people.note: Lead author of DDPM (2020), classifier-free guidance and the first video diffusion papers.

people.name: Robin Rombach
people.note: Lead author of latent diffusion, the compressed-space method behind Stable Diffusion and most video models.

people.name: Saining Xie
people.note: Co-created the diffusion transformer (DiT) with William Peebles, the design later scaled up for video.

people.name: Devi Parikh
people.note: A research director on Make-A-Video (2022), one of the first text-to-video diffusion systems.

people.name: Sasha Luccioni
people.role: AI and climate researcher, Hugging Face
people.note: Co-wrote the 2025 study showing that doubling an AI video's length roughly quadruples its energy use.

series.title: Longest clips reported by notable video models
series.caption: From about one second in 2016 to minutes in 2024. Figures for company models are as reported by the companies.

points.label: VGAN: 32 frames, up to about 1 second
Imagen Video: 128 frames at 24 fps, about 5.3 seconds

series.title: Pixels in one generated clip
series.caption: Width × height × frames. It grew more than 50,000-fold in eight years, which is why video models must compress before they generate.

points.label: Kling: 1920 × 1080 × 3,600 frames (2 minutes at 30 fps, reported maximum)

facts: At 24 frames per second, one minute of film is 1,440 separate pictures.
One open video model used about 3.4 million joules to make a 5-second clip, more than 700 times the energy of a high-quality AI image, MIT Technology Review found in 2025.
A 2025 Hugging Face study found that doubling the length of an AI video roughly quadruples the energy it takes to make.
HunyuanVideo's autoencoder shrinks each frame 8 times in width and height and 4 times in time, so the model works on about 48 times fewer numbers than the raw video.
The word "deepfake" comes from the username of the Reddit account that posted face-swapped videos in 2017.
